evidence: The same accounts that document the Juno-60 purchase name the TR-909 as the other half of Heard's setup when he recorded 'Can You Feel It', 'Mystery of Love' and 'Washing Machine' in 1984.

trackPair.whatToListenFor: The drum machine carries this record almost on its own. Listen to the hi-hats: bright and metallic, ticking in a perfectly even grid over a synthetic kick. The 909's cymbals were short digital recordings, which is why they sound harder and more real than the rest of the kit. Then play 'Can You Feel It', made on the same two machines in the same few days, and hear how differently they can be used.

explanation: Larry Heard's drum machine was a Roland 909, the same model that reached Frankie Knuckles from Detroit that same year. On 'Washing Machine' the 909 is almost the whole song, and comparing it with 'Can You Feel It' shows how one small setup could make very different records. The two Chicago connections from the 909 in the same year show the machine arriving by different routes: a DJ's live tool for Knuckles, a bedroom composer's instrument for Heard. That pairing is part of why house has both a club side and a more inward-looking one.
demoCaption: Same beat, same speed, two Roland drum machines: only the machine changes between A and B. B is the 909, the machine Larry Heard used in 1984. Listen to its hi-hat, brighter and harder than the 808's. On the real 909 the hi-hats and cymbals were short samples while the drums were analog circuits, which is part of why they cut through on Heard's records. On 'Washing Machine' the 909 carries almost the whole record. Both kits here are synthesized, the 909's hats included.
